drills.los_text: discuss common characteristics of institutional investors as a group

questions.stem: Global asset management industry assets under management as of 2020 most likely reached:

options.B: approximately USD 500 trillion.
options.C: approximately USD 10 trillion.

rationales.A: On a global basis, the total value of assets under management by the asset management industry as of 2020 reached more than USD 100 trillion, and as such the industry wields significant influence over capital markets. Within that total, pension plans account for approximately US$57 trillion in investable assets, or roughly half of global institutional assets under management; sovereign wealth funds account for about US$8 trillion as of the end of 2020; endowments and foundations account for approximately US$1.6 trillion; and banks and insurance companies comprise net financial assets on the order of US$9 trillion.
rationales.B: USD 500 trillion overstates the industry several-fold. The 2020 scale is more than USD 100 trillion, of which pension plans alone account for roughly US$57 trillion, sovereign wealth funds about US$8 trillion, endowments and foundations approximately US$1.6 trillion, and banks and insurers on the order of US$9 trillion in net financial assets.
rationales.C: USD 10 trillion is an order of magnitude too small. Pension plans on their own hold roughly US$57 trillion in investable assets, about half of global institutional assets under management, and total industry assets under management exceeded USD 100 trillion as of 2020.

questions.stem: The five common defining characteristics of institutional investors as a group are most likely:

options.A: scale, long horizon, guaranteed government backing, governance, principal–agent issues.
options.B: scale, short liquidity-driven horizon, regulation, governance, principal–agent issues.
options.C: scale, long horizon, regulation, governance, principal–agent issues.

rationales.A: Institutional investors have no guaranteed government backing; that is true of neither pension plans, endowments, foundations, banks, nor insurers as a class. The characteristic this list displaces is regulatory frameworks: institutional investors must contend with multiple regulatory regimes, which shape permissible assets, funding requirements, and disclosure.
rationales.B: The horizon is long term, not short. It is generally determined by a specific liability stream, and the relatively low liquidity needs that follow from it are what allow institutions to hold private equity, private real estate, infrastructure, and other illiquid assets. A short-term horizon driven by liquidity needs is not a defining characteristic of institutional investors as a group, although particular cases such as a frozen defined benefit plan in de-risking mode are exceptions.
rationales.C: The common defining characteristics of institutional investors are: scale, that is, asset size, which ranges from less than US$25 million to more than US$10 billion; a long-term investment horizon, often determined by a specific liability stream; regulatory frameworks, since institutional investors must contend with multiple regimes; a governance framework, because institutions typically implement their investment programs through an investment office with a clearly defined governance model; and principal–agent issues, which must be recognized and managed appropriately because institutions manage assets on behalf of others.

questions.stem: With respect to scale, the smallest institutional investors are most likely characterized by:

options.A: less reliance on external managers and consultants than large funds.
options.B: no scale-related constraints on portfolio construction.
options.C: limited access to high-minimum asset classes and greater reliance on external managers.

rationales.A: The opposite holds. Because small institutions face challenges hiring skilled investment professionals, they are more likely, not less, to outsource investments to external asset managers and to rely on investment consultants. Light internal staffing is the reason for the outsourcing, not a substitute for it.
rationales.B: High minimum investment sizes and internal resource requirements constrain small funds materially. Platforms and intermediaries do not give an institution with less than US$25 million the same access to private equity or property as one with more than US$10 billion, and the smaller institution also faces the harder task of hiring skilled investment professionals.
rationales.C: Institutional assets under management range from relatively small, for example less than US$25 million, to relatively large, for example more than US$10 billion. Smaller institutions may face challenges in building a diversified portfolio spanning public and private asset classes because they may be unable to access certain investments that have a high minimum investment size; they are less likely, for instance, to be able to invest in private equity or in real estate, that is, property. Small institutional investors may also face challenges in hiring skilled investment professionals. As a result, they are more likely to outsource investments to external asset managers and to rely on investment consultants.

questions.stem: The largest institutional investors are most likely characterized by:

options.A: economies of scale with no offsetting costs.
options.B: diseconomies of scale that can rule out niche allocations such as venture capital.
options.C: an overweight to niche strategies such as venture capital.

rationales.A: Diseconomies emerge at the top end, so scale brings offsetting costs. Niche allocations can be too small relative to total assets to justify their due diligence costs, some external strategies are capacity constrained, and sizable trading orders incur market impact costs.
rationales.B: The largest institutional investors may experience diseconomies of scale. They might be unable to invest in certain niche investments such as venture capital: given the size of the assets under management, a small allocation to venture capital may not generate sufficient returns to justify the position, including its due diligence costs. The largest institutional investors may also be unable to deploy as much capital as desired with some external managers, because certain investment strategies are capacity constrained. To overcome these constraints, some of the largest institutions buy private companies, property, and infrastructure assets directly and manage their traditional asset-class portfolios in house. Large institutional investors also face the costs of market impact, given their sizable trading orders.
rationales.C: The reverse holds. For a very large fund, a venture capital allocation small enough to fit the capacity of the niche cannot generate returns sufficient to justify the position and its due diligence costs, so the largest investors frequently cannot pursue such strategies at all rather than overweighting them. Capacity constraints at external managers work the same way.

questions.stem: Pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, endowments, and foundations typically have long investment horizons and relatively low liquidity needs. Their net cash outlays as a percentage of assets under management are most likely:

options.B: above 30%.
options.C: 5% or less.

rationales.A: Net outflows do exist. These institutions make net payouts to beneficiaries, sponsors, or grantees; those payouts are relatively modest as a percentage of assets under management, typically around 5% or less, but they are not zero, and a frozen defined benefit plan in de-risking mode can need considerably more.
rationales.B: Net payouts are much lower than 30%, typically around 5% or less of assets under management. Outlays at 30% would preclude the broad allocations to private equity, private real estate, natural resources, infrastructure, and hedge funds that these institutions are able to hold precisely because their liquidity needs are low.
rationales.C: Pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, endowments, and foundations all typically have long investment horizons and relatively low liquidity needs. Cash outlays are relatively modest as a percentage of assets under management, with net payouts typically around 5% or less. There are exceptions: a frozen defined benefit plan, for example, might be in a de-risking mode that increases its liquidity needs. Relatively low liquidity needs allow these institutions to invest in a broad range of alternative asset classes, including private equity, private real estate, natural resources, infrastructure, and hedge funds.

questions.stem: Banks and insurance companies differ from other institutional investors most likely because they:

options.A: are less regulated than other institutional investors.
options.B: are more asset/liability focused, within tight capital adequacy rules.
options.C: are subject to no regulatory oversight of their investments.

rationales.A: Banks and insurance companies are more tightly regulated than other institutional investors, not less. Capital adequacy rules constrain which assets they may hold and how much risk those assets may carry, so lighter regulation is the opposite of what sets them apart.
rationales.B: Banks and insurance companies function as financial intermediaries, balancing assets, loans, and derivatives so that they can meet the claims of depositors, counterparties, policyholders, and creditors while still earning an adequate return on capital. They therefore tend to be much more asset/liability focused than other institutional investors, and they pursue that focus while operating within tight regulations designed to ensure adequacy of capital. Pension funds, endowments, and sovereign wealth funds are by comparison more asset-focused, with liability considerations less central to the allocation decision.
rationales.C: Regulatory oversight of these firms' investment activities is extensive rather than absent. The distinguishing feature is an asset/liability focus pursued inside strict capital adequacy regulation, so assuming no oversight removes the very constraint that shapes their investment behavior.

questions.stem: From the 1970s to the present, institutional asset allocation most likely has evolved in the order:

options.A: international equities, alternatives, 60/40 equity/fixed income, domestic fixed income.
options.B: 60/40 equity/fixed income, domestic fixed income, alternatives, international equities.
options.C: domestic fixed income, 60/40 equity/fixed income, international equities, alternatives.

rationales.A: This reverses the actual progression. Allocations ran from domestic fixed income in the 1970s, to a strategic 60% equity/40% fixed income mix in the 1980s, to international equities in the 1990s, to increased allocations to alternative assets in the 21st century. Placing international equities first and domestic fixed income last inverts that history.
rationales.B: The order is scrambled. Domestic, fixed-income instruments dominated pension and endowment portfolios in the 1970s; the 60% equity/40% fixed income strategic allocation emerged in the 1980s; international equity diversification followed in the 1990s; and the move into alternatives is a 21st-century development, not a 1990s one.
rationales.C: In the 1970s most pensions and endowments invested almost exclusively in domestic, fixed-income instruments. In the 1980s many institutional investors began to invest in equity markets and often pursued a long-term strategic allocation of 60% equities and 40% fixed income. In the 1990s investors recognized the benefits of diversification and many made their first forays into international equity markets. At the turn of the 21st century, many of the world's largest pension funds and endowments diversified further and increased investments in alternative asset classes, including private equity, hedge funds, real estate, and other illiquid assets. Alongside that sequence, pension plans have moved toward liability-driven investing, sovereign wealth funds have innovated with active management, and endowments have adopted the endowment model.

questions.stem: The principal-agent problem in institutional investing most likely arises when:

options.A: principals, rather than agents, make all investment decisions.
options.B: an agent decides on behalf of a principal and their interests are not aligned.
options.C: no conflict of interest exists between the parties.

rationales.A: Institutional investors almost never make every decision in-house. Operational and investment complexity forces them to rely on agents: internally, investment committee members and investment staff; externally, third-party asset managers, broker/dealers, consultants, and board members. That pervasive reliance on agents is what creates the principal-agent problem, so the problem cannot be assumed away by having principals decide everything themselves.
rationales.B: The principal-agent issue arises when one person, the agent, makes decisions on behalf of another person or institution, the principal, and their interests are not aligned. A dilemma exists for the agent when he or she may be motivated to act in his or her own best interests and not in the best interests of the principal. Because of operational and investment complexity, institutional investors generally rely on various parties, that is, agents, to act on their behalf. Agents may be internal or external: internal agents include investment committee members and investment staff, while external agents include third-party asset managers, broker/dealers, consultants, and board members.
rationales.C: This states the condition backwards. The conflict is the problem: it exists precisely because the agent's interests diverge from the principal's. Where no conflict of interest exists, the agent's incentives and the principal's objectives coincide and no principal-agent problem arises.

questions.stem: A hedge fund fee structure illustrates the principal-agent problem most likely because:

options.A: a high base fee is due regardless of performance, giving little incentive to outperform.
options.B: managers understate assets under management to reduce the fees reported to clients.
options.C: a low base fee forces excessive risk taking to earn the incentive fee.

rationales.A: A typical example of the principal-agent problem is a performance fee structure designed by an external fund manager to provide attractive compensation through a high base fee, which is due regardless of fund performance. Because the manager is paid substantially whether or not results are good, the structure gives little incentive for the fund manager to produce superior performance. Such fee arrangements are common among hedge funds and have led to greater demand for fee transparency and for alignment of interest between hedge fund managers and their clients.
rationales.B: The conflict here is not misreporting of assets under management or of the fees charged on them. It is that a high base fee is collected regardless of fund performance, which leaves the manager with little incentive to produce superior results for clients.
rationales.C: The structure at issue features a high base fee that is due regardless of performance, not a low one. The resulting problem is a weak incentive to outperform; excessive risk taking driven by reliance on an incentive fee is a different conflict and not the one this fee structure illustrates.

drills.los_text: discuss investment policy of institutional investors

questions.stem: An institutional investor's IPS most likely codifies:

options.B: management compensation arrangements.
options.C: day-to-day trading strategies and security selections.

rationales.A: Institutional investors codify their mission, investment objectives, and guidelines in an investment policy statement, which establishes policies and procedures for the effective administration and management of the institutional assets. Besides mission and investment objectives, that is, return and risk tolerance, the IPS should cover any constraints that affect the asset allocation, the asset allocation policy with ranges and asset class benchmarks, the rebalancing policy, guidelines affecting the implementation of the asset allocation policy, and reporting requirements. A well-crafted IPS also helps minimize principal-agent challenges by providing clear guidance on day-to-day management of the assets.
rationales.B: Compensation of staff and external managers is a governance and administrative matter that sits outside the investment-policy scope of the IPS, which addresses mission, objectives, constraints, allocation policy with ranges and benchmarks, rebalancing, and reporting.
rationales.C: Trading tactics and individual security decisions sit below the IPS. The document sets the mission, investment objectives, asset allocation policy with ranges and asset class benchmarks, rebalancing policy, implementation guidelines, and reporting requirements, and leaves day-to-day implementation to the parties it guides.

questions.stem: For banks and insurance companies, the investment objective is most likely:

options.A: to minimize the volatility of asset values.
options.B: to maximize the expected return on the asset portfolio.
options.C: to maximize net present value by balancing asset returns against liability costs and risks.

rationales.A: Minimizing the volatility of asset values looks at only one side of the balance sheet. The objective is net present value maximization, which balances expected asset returns against the expected cost of liabilities and the overall risks of both, within regulatory capital constraints.
rationales.B: Maximizing the expected return on the asset portfolio alone ignores the expected cost of liabilities, the overall risks of assets and liabilities, and the capital adequacy rules these firms operate under.
rationales.C: For banks and insurance companies, the investment objective is to maximize net present value by balancing (i) the expected returns on assets, (ii) the expected cost of liabilities, (iii) the overall risks of assets and liabilities, and (iv) the economic relationships between and among assets and liabilities. All four elements matter jointly: a portfolio that raises expected asset returns while worsening the asset/liability relationship, or while straining capital adequacy, does not improve net present value.

questions.stem: Risk tolerance for institutional investors most likely is expressed as:

options.A: value at risk with scenario-based stress tests, for defined benefit pension funds.
options.B: surplus volatility, for defined benefit pension funds.
options.C: surplus volatility, for endowments and foundations.

rationales.A: Value at risk, conditional value at risk, and comprehensive, scenario-based stress tests are how banks and insurance companies express risk tolerance. Defined benefit pension funds use surplus volatility, the standard deviation of asset returns in excess of liability returns, so this pairing attaches the wrong measure to the wrong type of investor.
rationales.B: Risk tolerance is expressed differently by type of institutional investor. Defined benefit pension funds use surplus volatility, the standard deviation of asset returns in excess of liability returns. Sovereign wealth funds use the probability of investment losses, or of not maintaining purchasing power, over a certain time period. Endowments and foundations use volatility of total returns, the standard deviation of total returns. Banks and insurance companies use value at risk or conditional value at risk together with comprehensive, scenario-based stress tests.
rationales.C: Surplus volatility is the defined benefit pension fund measure, because a pension plan's risk is the mismatch between asset returns and liability returns. Endowments and foundations express risk tolerance as the volatility of total returns, the standard deviation of total returns, so this pairing is misassigned.

questions.stem: The Norway Model is most likely characterized by:

options.B: largely passive holdings of public equities and fixed income, with few alternatives.
options.C: heavy exposure to alternatives and private markets.

rationales.A: Public equities are central to the Norway model rather than absent from it: the traditional 60% equity/40% fixed income portfolio falls under this model, held largely passively and within tight tracking error limits.
rationales.B: The Norway model, popularized by Norway's Government Pension Fund Global, is characterized by an almost exclusive reliance on public equities and fixed income; the traditional 60/40 equity/bond model falls under it. Assets are largely passively managed, usually within tight tracking error limits, with very little to no allocation to alternative investments. The advantages of this approach are that investment costs and fees are low, investments are transparent, the risk of poor manager selection is low, and there is little complexity for a governing board. The disadvantage is that there is limited potential for value added.
rationales.C: Heavy exposure to alternatives and private markets describes the endowment model. The Norway model is nearly all public markets, largely passive, with very little to no allocation to alternatives.

questions.stem: The Endowment Model is most likely characterized by:

options.A: passive, benchmark-hugging management with no alternatives.
options.B: wholly internal management, with no external managers.
options.C: significant alternatives exposure, active management, and external managers.

rationales.A: Passive, benchmark-hugging management with no alternatives describes the Norway model, which relies almost exclusively on public equities and fixed income held within tight tracking error limits. The endowment approach is its opposite.
rationales.B: External management is characteristic of the endowment model rather than absent from it: the model outsources implementation to external managers, particularly in private markets and hedge funds.
rationales.C: The endowment model, popularized by Yale under David Swensen, is characterized by significant exposure to alternative investments such as private markets and hedge funds, significant active management, and externally managed assets. Its advantage is high value-added potential; its drawbacks are that it is expensive and, for most sovereign wealth funds, difficult to implement given their large asset sizes.

questions.stem: The Canada Model differs from the Endowment Model most likely by:

options.A: relying more heavily on external asset managers and consultants.
options.B: relying more on internally managed assets.
options.C: replacing active management with a passive reference portfolio.

rationales.A: The direction is reversed. Heavy reliance on external asset managers and consultants is the endowment model's hallmark; the Canada model's distinguishing feature is insourcing, with more assets managed internally.
rationales.B: The Canada model, popularized by the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, resembles the endowment model in its high allocation to alternatives, but unlike the endowment model it relies more on internally managed assets. Its innovative features are the reference portfolio, a passive mix of public equities, fixed income, and cash that is cheap and easily implementable and is expected to achieve the long-term expected return consistent with the institution's investment objectives and risk appetite; the total portfolio approach, which constructs the portfolio so that planned risk exposures at the total portfolio level are maintained as individual investments enter, leave, or change in value; and active management, ranging from tilting the asset allocation through to security selection.
rationales.C: The reference portfolio is a passive, risk-equivalent benchmark, not the portfolio actually held. The Canada model manages actively against it, from tilting the asset allocation down to security selection, so active management is retained rather than eliminated.

questions.stem: The liability-driven investing (LDI) model is most likely focused on:

options.A: hedging liabilities with duration-matched fixed income.
options.B: maximizing asset-only total return.
options.C: hedging liabilities with short-duration instruments.

rationales.A: The LDI model hedges the liabilities and the interest rate risk they carry through duration-matched fixed-income exposure. It has gained significant importance, particularly among corporate defined benefit pension plans in the United States. In the LDI model the primary investment objective is to generate returns sufficient to cover liabilities, so the investor's focus shifts away from an asset-only context toward maximizing expected surplus return, the excess return of assets over liabilities, and managing surplus volatility. Implementations often separate the portfolio into a hedging portfolio, which hedges the main risk factor in the liabilities (interest rate risk) using long-duration fixed income and sometimes interest rate swaps to extend duration, and a return-generating portfolio holding public equities and alternatives. LDI portfolios other than those of banks and insurance institutions typically have significant exposure to long-duration fixed-income securities.
rationales.B: LDI shifts the focus away from an asset-only context toward maximizing expected surplus return and managing surplus volatility. The liabilities drive the strategy and define the objective: returns must be sufficient to cover them. They are not a soft benchmark against which an independently maximized asset-only total return is later compared.
rationales.C: Because pension liabilities are long duration, LDI portfolios typically hold significant long-duration fixed income, sometimes extending duration further with interest rate swaps, so that the hedging portfolio's interest rate sensitivity matches that of the liabilities. Short-duration instruments would minimize the price volatility of the assets considered alone while leaving a large duration mismatch against the liabilities, which raises surplus volatility rather than reducing it.

questions.stem: The inflation metric used to express an institutional investor's return target in real terms is most likely:

options.B: defined as the consumer price index.
options.C: left undefined.

rationales.A: When the return target is expressed in real terms, the relevant inflation metric must be defined, and the appropriate metric is specific to the institution and its cost base. GIC, Singapore's sovereign wealth fund, uses global inflation defined as G3 inflation: the United States, Japan, and the Eurozone. The Future Fund of Australia targets CPI plus 4% to 5%. Some US endowments use the Higher Education Price Index (HEPI) published by Commonfund, because the costs they fund track higher education costs rather than general consumer prices. These investor-specific choices matter, because the metric chosen sets the hurdle the portfolio must clear.
rationales.B: The consumer price index is only one of the metrics in use, and for several investors it is the wrong one. GIC uses G3 inflation across the United States, Japan, and the Eurozone; some US endowments use the Higher Education Price Index published by Commonfund; the Future Fund of Australia targets CPI plus 4% to 5%. The metric must be appropriate to the institution rather than applied uniformly.
rationales.C: The metric is defined rather than left open. Expressing a return target in real terms requires specifying the inflation measure the return has to exceed, and institutions do specify one: G3 inflation at GIC, the Higher Education Price Index at some US endowments, and CPI plus 4% to 5% at the Future Fund of Australia.

drills.los_text: discuss the stakeholders in the portfolio, the liabilities, the investment time horizons, and the liquidity needs of different types of institutional investors

questions.stem: The two main types of pension plans are most likely:

options.B: public and private.
options.C: cash and bond.

rationales.A: There are two main types of pension plans: defined benefit, in which the plan sponsor commits to paying a specified retirement benefit, and defined contribution, in which contributions are defined but the ultimate retirement benefit is not specified or guaranteed by the plan sponsor. The distinction determines who bears the investment risk. Under a defined benefit plan the sponsor assumes it, which is why the sponsor's own balance sheet and the plan's funded status drive the investment policy. Under a defined contribution plan the individual participant bears it, which is why plan design focuses on the menu of options and the default option.
rationales.B: Public versus private describes the plan sponsor, a government body or a corporation, not the type of plan. Either kind of sponsor can run either kind of plan. The two main plan types are defined benefit and defined contribution, distinguished by whether a specified retirement benefit is promised and therefore by whether the sponsor or the participant bears the investment risk.
rationales.C: Cash and bonds are asset classes a plan may hold, not types of pension plan. The two main types are defined benefit, under which the sponsor commits to a specified benefit and assumes the investment risk, and defined contribution, under which contributions are defined but the benefit is not guaranteed.

questions.stem: Compared with open mature plans, frozen defined benefit pension plans are most likely to:

options.B: have higher liquidity needs.
options.C: have lower liquidity needs.

rationales.A: A freeze stops new benefits from accruing, but it does not stop benefit payments to existing beneficiaries. Those ongoing payments create significant and persistent liquidity demands, which are met by holding more cash and other liquid investments.
rationales.B: Frozen defined benefit plans often experience negative cash flow, because benefit payments exceed contributions, and so must hold even more cash and other liquid investments than open mature plans. Such plans are typically in de-risking mode as well. More generally, the more mature a pension fund, the shorter its investment horizon, and the horizon directly affects risk tolerance and the allocation between fixed-income assets and riskier assets.
rationales.C: Liquidity needs are higher, not lower. No new benefits accrue, but benefit payments to existing beneficiaries continue while contributions shrink, producing negative cash flow that has to be funded out of the portfolio. Frozen plans therefore hold more cash and other liquid investments than open mature plans, not less.

questions.stem: Under Australia's Superannuation Guarantee, the employer contribution to an employee's retirement savings is most likely:

options.B: 9.5% of salary, voluntary.
options.C: 0% of salary.

rationales.A: In Australia most employees are covered by the defined contribution Superannuation Guarantee, under which employers must contribute 9.5% of an employee's salary. Because many participants do not actively make investment decisions, the government applies strict licensing and other obligations on trustees offering the default option, MySuper. Those obligations include providing a single diversified investment strategy as a default option suitable for the majority of participants, avoiding unnecessary or excessive fees, and delivering value for money, measured by long-term net returns.
rationales.B: The 9.5% contribution is mandatory, not voluntary. The Superannuation Guarantee obliges employers to contribute, which is what makes coverage near universal, and the system is tightly regulated around that obligation: trustees offering the MySuper default option face licensing requirements covering the default strategy, fees, and value for money, precisely because participation is not left to employee or employer initiative.
rationales.C: A zero contribution is not permitted. Employers must contribute 9.5% of the employee's salary under the Superannuation Guarantee, which covers most Australian employees, and the default option for those who do not choose investments is itself regulated through the MySuper licensing obligations.

questions.stem: Budget stabilization funds, savings funds, and pension reserve funds are three of the five sovereign wealth fund types in the IMF classification. The remaining two types are most likely:

options.B: infrastructure debt funds and reserve funds.
options.C: development funds and currency hedging funds.

rationales.A: Sovereign wealth funds fall into five types under the IMF classification, each with a different investment horizon, liability structure, and liquidity profile. Budget stabilization funds insulate the fiscal budget from commodity price volatility; their liabilities are uncertain and their horizon short, so they hold mainly government bonds. Development funds support economic development, often through infrastructure. Savings funds transform the proceeds of non-renewable natural resources into long-term diversified wealth for future generations. Reserve funds aim to reduce the negative carry of holding foreign exchange reserves. Pension reserve funds prefund contingent pension liabilities.
rationales.B: Infrastructure debt funds are not one of the five IMF categories. The missing type is development funds, which support economic development and often do so through infrastructure projects, but as a development mandate rather than a debt fund category. Reserve funds, which aim to reduce the negative carry of holding foreign exchange reserves, do belong on the list.
rationales.C: Currency hedging funds are not one of the five IMF categories. The missing type is reserve funds, whose purpose is to reduce the negative carry of holding foreign exchange reserves; that is a reserve management objective rather than a currency hedging mandate. Development funds, which support economic development through infrastructure and similar projects, do belong on the list.

questions.stem: Under its fiscal spending rule, the share of fund value that Norway's Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG) intends to withdraw annually is closest to:

rationales.A: The fund does spend. Its fiscal spending rule provides for a structured annual withdrawal of 3% of fund value, with the goal of gradually phasing oil revenue into the Norwegian economy, so a zero withdrawal describes neither the rule nor the fund's purpose.
rationales.B: Norway's Government Pension Fund Global uses a fiscal spending rule whereby it intends to withdraw 3% of the fund's value annually, with the goal of gradually phasing oil revenue into the Norwegian economy. The 3% rate is not arbitrary: it is linked to the expected real return earned by the GPFG. Setting the spending rate at the expected real return allows the fund to support the budget while preserving its real value for future generations.
rationales.C: A 10% annual withdrawal would far exceed the fund's expected real return and would steadily erode its real value. The spending rule sets withdrawals at 3% of fund value, a rate deliberately linked to the expected real return the GPFG earns.

questions.stem: The hybrid rule, commonly called the Yale spending rule, is one of the three main endowment spending policies. The other two are most likely:

options.A: the constant growth rule and the market value rule.
options.B: the constant growth rule and the fixed nominal payout rule.
options.C: the market value rule and the realized gains rule.

rationales.A: The three main endowment spending policies are the constant growth rule, the market value rule, and the hybrid rule. Under the constant growth rule, the endowment provides a fixed amount annually to the university, typically adjusted for inflation, with the inflation rate usually based on the Higher Education Price Index (HEPI); it is commonly complemented with caps and floors, typically between 4% and 6% of average assets under management over one or three years. Under the market value rule, the endowment pays a pre-specified percentage, the spending rate, typically between 4% and 6% of a moving average of asset values, usually smoothed over three to five years. Under the hybrid rule, spending is a weighted average of the constant growth and market value rules, which is why it is commonly referred to as the Yale spending rule.
rationales.B: A fixed nominal payout is not one of the three policies. The missing rule is the market value rule, which pays a pre-specified percentage, typically 4% to 6%, of a three- to five-year moving average of asset values. A fixed nominal amount would erode purchasing power over time, which is exactly why the constant growth rule adjusts its fixed amount for inflation, usually by the Higher Education Price Index.
rationales.C: There is no realized gains spending rule; endowment spending is not tied to realized capital gains, which would make the payout hostage to portfolio turnover. The missing policy is the constant growth rule, under which a fixed amount is provided annually and adjusted for inflation, commonly with caps and floors of roughly 4% to 6% of average assets under management.

questions.stem: To maintain intergenerational purchasing power, a university endowment's long-term return target is closest to:

options.B: 8% to 10% nominal.
options.C: 2% to 3% real.

rationales.A: The goal of providing intergenerational equity means university endowments aim to maintain their purchasing power, so they target a real rate of return, after inflation, equal to or greater than their spending rate. Given that endowments pay out on average between 4% and 6% of assets annually, they typically target a 5% to 5.5% real long-term rate of return. Net spending is closer to 2% to 4% of assets once gifts and donations are counted, but the real return target is set against the gross payout so that purchasing power passes through intact to future generations.
rationales.B: The target is stated in real terms, not nominal, precisely because maintaining intergenerational purchasing power requires netting out inflation. The endowment sets a real return at or above its spending rate, typically about 5% to 5.5% given gross payouts of 4% to 6% of assets. A nominal target with no inflation adjustment leaves the endowment's real value exposed to whatever inflation turns out to be, and for endowments the relevant inflation measure is often the Higher Education Price Index rather than CPI.
rationales.C: Net spending after gifts and donations is indeed closer to 2% to 4% of assets, but the real return target is set at or above the gross payout rate of 4% to 6%, typically 5% to 5.5% real. Gifts and donations cannot be relied on to fund spending, so the endowment's own assets must earn enough in real terms to cover the full payout and still maintain purchasing power.

questions.stem: The share of asset value that a US private grant-making foundation must distribute annually in grants is most likely:

options.C: any share the foundation chooses.

rationales.A: A 5% minimum applies. In the United States, private grant-making foundations enjoy the same tax-exempt status as endowments, but unlike endowments they face minimum payout requirements, and distributing nothing would subject the foundation to a 30% tax on undistributed income.
rationales.B: In the United States, private grant-making foundations enjoy the same tax-exempt status as endowments. Unlike endowments, such private foundations are subject to minimum payout, or spending, requirements: they must distribute a minimum of 5% of their asset value on an annual basis in grants that support their mission. Failing to meet this spending requirement subjects the foundation to a 30% tax on undistributed income. Most tax-exempt private foundations also pay an excise tax of 2% on their net investment income, so the mandated payout and the tax drag together set the return the portfolio has to earn.
rationales.C: The 5% payout is mandatory, not discretionary. A foundation that distributes less than 5% of its asset value in grants over the year is subject to a 30% tax on undistributed income, so the spending rate is fixed by the requirement rather than chosen by the foundation; only spending above the minimum is a matter of discretion.

questions.stem: The liability stream faced by life insurers is most likely characterized by:

options.B: long duration.
options.C: short duration.

rationales.A: Life insurers carry substantial liabilities against their investment portfolios: policy benefits, annuity payments, and retirement plan obligations. The liability stream is the central input to the return objective and to the amount of investment risk the insurer can tolerate, so treating a life insurer as having no meaningful liabilities misstates its basic position.
rationales.B: Life insurance companies have historically set portfolio return objectives with long time horizons of 20 to 40 years, so they face a liability stream and investment horizon of long duration. Life insurance spans a range of products, including individual life, group life and disability, individual annuity, and retirement plan products. Term life involves a one-time payout with high predictability, while annuity products involve an ongoing payout of shorter duration that is subject to longevity risk. The nature of the liability stream has important implications for the amount of investment risk that can be tolerated.
rationales.C: Short duration describes property and casualty insurers rather than life insurers. A life insurer's obligations run over 20 to 40 year horizons, so the duration of the liability stream is very long, not short.

questions.stem: The liability stream faced by property and casualty (P&C) insurers is most likely characterized by:

options.B: long duration and high predictability.
options.C: short duration and high volatility.

rationales.A: Claims are the liabilities of a P&C insurer, and they are substantial. P&C policies are written against low-probability, potentially high-cost events such as hurricanes and other natural disasters, so the insurer holds a real and highly uncertain claim obligation against its investment portfolio.
rationales.B: Long, predictable duration describes life insurers, whose return objectives have historically been set over 20 to 40 year horizons. P&C liabilities are the opposite: shorter duration and highly volatile, because the underlying events are infrequent and their cost is uncertain.
rationales.C: In general, P&C insurers face a shorter-duration liability stream and investment horizon than life insurers. P&C insurance involves events with a lower probability of occurrence and potentially higher cost, especially natural disasters, which makes business claims highly volatile. The result is a liability stream with short duration and high uncertainty: a P&C insurer may, for example, initiate policies against catastrophic events such as hurricanes. Because of the law of large numbers, P&C insurers may benefit from developing global, diversified portfolios that are more amenable to statistical analysis.

drills.los_text: describe the focus of legal, regulatory, and tax constraints affecting different types of institutional investors

questions.stem: The Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) is most likely best described as a law that:

options.B: eliminates pension regulation.
options.C: regulates vesting, funding, and payouts of US corporate pension plans.

rationales.A: ERISA applies to plans, not to individuals. It sets the standards that US corporate pension plans and their fiduciaries must meet, including a fiduciary code of conduct and required disclosures, rather than governing the personal investment arrangements of individual savers.
rationales.B: ERISA is a robust regulatory regime, not a removal of regulation. US corporate pension plans are subject to significant regulatory oversight: ERISA governs vesting, funding requirements, and payouts, imposes a fiduciary code of conduct and disclosure obligations, and created a federal guaranty agency.
rationales.C: ERISA regulates vesting, funding requirements, and payouts for US corporate pension plans, and includes a fiduciary code of conduct and required disclosures. It also established the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation, a US government agency that collects premiums from pension plan sponsors and pays benefits to participants, approximately 630,000 of them, in terminated plans.

questions.stem: The US Pension Protection Act of 2006 is most likely to have:

options.A: shifted defined benefit funding oversight to the individual states.
options.B: lowered the discount rates permitted on plan liabilities.
options.C: established minimum funding standards for defined benefit plans.

rationales.A: The act established federal minimum funding standards for defined benefit plans. It did not devolve funding oversight to the individual states; the standards and the subsequent revisions to permitted discount rates operate at the federal level.
rationales.B: The direction is reversed. Later revisions raised the rates corporations could use to discount their liabilities, set as high-grade bond yields averaged over 25 years. Higher discount rates reduce the reported present value of liabilities, so defined benefit plans must generate higher, not lower, returns for their funding status to remain sustainable, which typically requires taking on greater investment risk.
rationales.C: The US Pension Protection Act of 2006 established minimum funding standards for defined benefit plans, while later revisions raised the rates corporations could use to discount their liabilities, namely high-grade bond yields averaged over 25 years. A potential consequence of using higher discount rates is that these defined benefit plans must generate higher returns for their funding status to remain sustainable, which typically requires taking on greater investment risk.

questions.stem: The tax treatment of a participant's contributions to a US 401(k) plan is most likely:

options.B: tax deferral.
options.C: immediate taxation.

rationales.A: A 401(k) confers substantial tax benefits. Participants make pre-tax contributions and pay no tax on investment earnings as they accumulate, so the plan is materially more favorable than saving in a taxable account.
rationales.B: In the United States, 401(k) plans are tax deferred: participants make pre-tax contributions and do not pay tax on investment earnings. Benefit payments are instead taxed as ordinary income when received. To encourage savings retention within the pension plan, early withdrawals before age 59 and a half are taxed an additional 10%.
rationales.C: Contributions are made on a pre-tax basis, so tax is deferred rather than imposed immediately. Taxation occurs later, when benefit payments are received and taxed as ordinary income, with an additional 10% tax on early withdrawals before age 59 and a half.

questions.stem: The Uniform Prudent Management of Institutional Funds Act of 2006 (UPMIFA) is most likely to have:

options.A: expanded spending flexibility to adjust for market fluctuations.
options.B: left endowment spending and management unchanged.
options.C: removed spending flexibility from charitable organizations.

rationales.A: In the United States, endowments and foundations are governed by UPMIFA, which has two important features. First, it allows charitable organizations flexibility in spending decisions, which could be adjusted for fluctuations in the market value of assets; endowments in particular could meet the fiduciary standard of prudence by maintaining the purchasing power of the fund. Second, it modernizes the standard of prudence for the management of charitable funds by adopting the principles of modern portfolio theory established by the Uniform Prudent Investor Act of 1994.
rationales.B: UPMIFA reshaped US endowment governance through its two features: flexibility in spending decisions that can be adjusted for market value fluctuations, and a modernized standard of prudence based on modern portfolio theory as established by the Uniform Prudent Investor Act of 1994.
rationales.C: The act expanded flexibility rather than removing it. Charitable organizations were allowed flexibility in spending decisions that could be adjusted for fluctuations in the market value of assets, letting endowments meet the fiduciary standard of prudence by maintaining purchasing power.

questions.stem: With respect to the tax-exempt status of endowments and foundations, it is most likely that:

options.A: donations are deductible with no limit tied to the donor's adjusted gross income.
options.B: donations are deductible up to a percentage of the donor's adjusted gross income.
options.C: payouts are taxable to the receiving institution regardless of its tax status.

rationales.A: Deductibility is capped. Gifts and donations to endowments and foundations are usually tax-deductible for the person or entity making the gift only up to a certain percentage of adjusted gross income, not without limit.
rationales.B: Tax-exempt status has three elements. First, taxation of gifts and donations: gifts and donations to endowments and foundations are usually tax-deductible, up to a certain percentage of adjusted gross income, for the person or entity making them. Second, taxation of income and capital gains on assets: these are usually tax-exempt in countries that have endowments and charitable organizations. Third, taxation of payouts: payouts are tax-exempt if the receiving institution is exempt from income tax, but if payouts support the operating budget of a for-profit business, that business must treat the payout as taxable income.
rationales.C: Payouts are tax-exempt when the receiving institution is exempt from income tax. Only where payouts are made to support the operating budget of a for-profit business is the payout taxable, and then it is taxable to that business rather than universally.

questions.stem: The regulatory changes introduced by the updated European Institutions for Occupational Retirement Provision (IORP II) directive are most likely focused on:

options.B: capital requirements modeled on Solvency II.
options.C: no change from the preceding framework.

rationales.A: In Europe, the updated IORP II directive leads to regulatory changes for pension plans, and although each country interprets the provisions slightly differently, the changes relate to governance, risk management, and disclosure. A number of key functions are defined, such as internal audit, and standards are applied to those executing them, including a requirement that such a person does not carry out a similar function for the plan sponsor. Many pension plans will need to document their risk management policies and procedures: each fund must document its own risk assessment, covering items such as the risk of not meeting benefit obligations and operational risk, including administrative error or fraud. The directive also brings greater harmonization of pension benefit statements.
rationales.B: IORP II is not a Solvency II style capital regime for occupational pension funds. Its changes relate to governance, risk management, and disclosure: defined key functions such as internal audit, standards for those executing them, a documented own risk assessment, and more harmonized benefit statements.
rationales.C: IORP II updated the preceding framework. It defines key functions such as internal audit, applies standards to those executing them, requires documented risk management policies and an own risk assessment covering the risk of not meeting benefit obligations and operational risk, and harmonizes pension benefit statements.

questions.stem: Changes to the legal and regulatory frameworks faced by institutional investors following the 2007-2009 global financial crisis are most likely best described as:

options.A: transferring supervision of large institutions to industry self-regulation.
options.B: loosening capital rules in order to restore market liquidity.
options.C: tightening leverage, collateral, liquidity, and clearing requirements.

rationales.A: Oversight of large financial institutions expanded rather than being eliminated or handed to self-regulatory organizations. The reforms imposed leverage limits, enhanced collateral and liquidity requirements, central clearing, and proprietary trading restrictions, all supervised by public regulators.
rationales.B: The direction of the reforms was tightening, not loosening. Capital, collateral, and liquidity requirements were increased, proprietary trading was restricted under the Volcker Rule, and reporting was made more transparent.
rationales.C: The key drivers of the legal and regulatory frameworks faced by institutional investors are investor protection, safety and soundness of financial institutions, and integrity of financial markets. Changes to these frameworks following the 2007-2009 global financial crisis focused on leverage limits, enhanced collateral requirements, increased liquidity requirements, central clearing, proprietary trading limits, private equity limits, trading tax implementation, brokerage fee limits, compensation limits, and requirements for more transparent reporting. Examples include Dodd-Frank and the Volcker Rule and FATCA in the United States, and UCITS V, AIFMD, Solvency II, MiFID II, EMIR, the financial transaction tax, and PRIIPs in the European Union.

questions.stem: The key drivers of the legal and regulatory frameworks faced by institutional investors are most likely:

options.A: investor protection, return maximization, and market integrity.
options.B: investor protection, institutional safety and soundness, and market integrity.
options.C: investor protection, institutional safety and soundness, and tax revenue maximization.

rationales.A: Regulators do not target the maximization of market returns. The second driver is the safety and soundness of financial institutions, which is about solvency, capital, and liquidity rather than investment performance.
rationales.B: The key drivers of the legal and regulatory frameworks faced by institutional investors are investor protection, safety and soundness of financial institutions, and integrity of financial markets. These three drivers underlie global regulatory efforts, including those of IOSCO, which brings together 217 world securities regulators, of which 127 are national ordinary members.
rationales.C: Generating government tax revenue is not one of the drivers. The third driver is the integrity of financial markets, alongside investor protection and the safety and soundness of financial institutions.

drills.los_text: evaluate risk considerations of private defined benefit (DB) pension plans in relation to 1) plan funded status, 2) sponsor financial strength, 3) interactions between the sponsor's business and the fund's investments, 4) plan design, and 5) workforce characteristics

questions.stem: Compared with an otherwise similar underfunded plan, a defined benefit plan with a large funded surplus most likely has risk tolerance that is:

options.B: lower.
options.C: higher.

rationales.A: Funded status is one of the primary drivers of a defined benefit plan's risk tolerance, so tolerance is not invariant to the surplus or deficit position. A plan whose assets exceed the present value of its liabilities can absorb a drawdown without immediately triggering a funding shortfall, while an underfunded plan cannot. Treating the two plans as having equal risk tolerance ignores the cushion that funding level provides, and ignores the fact that funded status sits alongside sponsor financial strength, common risk exposures, plan features, and workforce characteristics as a standard tolerance factor.
rationales.B: The relationship runs in the opposite direction. A surplus is a cushion that absorbs investment losses, which supports greater rather than lower risk tolerance. The instinct to protect a surplus at all costs describes a particular sponsor's choice to de-risk and immunize an already well-funded plan; it is not the general relationship between funded status and risk tolerance, which is positive.
rationales.C: A higher pension surplus, or higher funded status, implies potentially greater risk tolerance: a well-funded plan has a cushion to absorb investment losses. With assets above liabilities, a drawdown does not immediately create a funding shortfall or force additional sponsor contributions, so the plan can accept more asset risk. An underfunded plan faces the opposite pressure. It must grow assets faster than liabilities, yet a further loss deepens the deficit and raises required contributions, so a more conservative allocation is appropriate. Funded status, measured as surplus or deficit, is therefore a standard risk-tolerance factor for a defined benefit plan.

questions.stem: Lower sponsor debt ratios and higher current and expected sponsor profitability most likely imply a defined benefit plan risk tolerance that is:

options.B: greater.
options.C: unchanged.

rationales.A: The relationship runs in the same direction, not the opposite one. A financially strong sponsor is better able to make contributions if plan assets fall short, so sponsor strength raises rather than reduces the plan's capacity to bear risk. Reversing the sign would imply that a highly levered, marginally profitable sponsor could support more asset risk in its plan, which is the opposite of the case.
rationales.B: Lower debt ratios and higher current and expected profitability imply greater risk tolerance, and large sponsor company size relative to pension plan size implies greater risk tolerance as well, because the sponsor can absorb potential contribution volatility. The factors considered are debt to total assets, current and expected profitability, and the size of the plan compared with the market capitalization of the sponsor company. A strong sponsor has a higher capacity to make contributions if needed, so a shortfall in plan assets is less likely to become a financial problem for the firm. A weak, highly levered sponsor whose plan is large relative to its own market capitalization has little room to fund a deficit and must hold a more conservative allocation.
rationales.C: Sponsor financial status has a substantial effect rather than none. The sponsor is the ultimate source of contributions, so its debt load, its current and expected profitability, and the size of the plan relative to the sponsor all determine how much asset risk the plan can carry.

questions.stem: The relationship between the correlation of sponsor operating results with pension asset returns and a defined benefit plan's risk tolerance is most likely:

options.B: positive.
options.C: negative.

rationales.A: The common-risk channel between sponsor and plan is directly relevant to risk tolerance, so the correlation is not a neutral factor. Whether sponsor stress and pension losses arrive together determines whether the sponsor can fund a deficit when one appears, which is exactly what risk tolerance has to reflect.
rationales.B: The direction is the opposite. Lower, not higher, correlation supports greater risk tolerance, because sponsor stress and plan losses are then less likely to coincide. High correlation means funded status deteriorates exactly when the core business is weakest and least able to contribute, so high correlation reduces tolerance.
rationales.C: The lower the correlation of sponsor operating results with pension asset returns, the greater the risk tolerance, all else equal, which is an inverse, or negative, relationship. If the plan sponsor's revenues are highly cyclical, it will not want plan funded status to deteriorate when the core business suffers from a cyclical downturn. In such cases the defined benefit plan's asset allocation would be modified to ensure adequate diversification, so as not to have significant exposure to assets highly correlated with the sponsor's core business or industry. In sum, it is desirable for plan assets to have low correlation with the sponsor's operating assets and high correlation with the plan's liabilities.

questions.stem: Provisions for early retirement and for lump-sum distributions most likely affect a defined benefit plan's risk tolerance by:

options.B: leaving it unchanged.
options.C: lowering it.

rationales.A: These features reduce risk tolerance rather than raising it. Optionality held by participants shortens the effective duration of plan liabilities and makes the timing of outflows less predictable, both of which argue for a more conservative, better-matched asset mix.
rationales.B: The effect is real, not neutral. Early retirement and lump-sum provisions change when benefits are paid, and therefore the duration and liquidity profile of the liability the assets must support.
rationales.C: Such plan features tend to reduce the duration of plan liabilities, implying lower risk tolerance, all else equal. A participant who may retire early or take a lump sum holds an option against the plan, which pulls expected cash outflows forward and shortens effective liability duration. The shortened horizon leaves less time to recover from adverse markets, and the uncertainty over when the option is exercised creates liquidity uncertainty. Together these call for more liquid, shorter-duration matching assets, which leaves less capacity for return-seeking risk.

questions.stem: A younger workforce and a higher proportion of active lives relative to retired lives most likely affect a defined benefit plan's risk tolerance by:

options.B: raising it.
options.C: lowering it.

rationales.A: Workforce age and the ratio of active lives to retired lives are standard risk-tolerance drivers, not neutral details. They determine how far away the benefit payments are, and therefore the plan's investment horizon and its near-term liquidity needs.
rationales.B: The younger the workforce and the greater the proportion of active lives, the greater the duration of plan liabilities and the greater the risk tolerance. Benefit payments lie further in the future, so the plan has a longer horizon over which to recover from adverse markets and less need to hold liquid, short-duration assets. The converse also holds: generally, the more mature a pension fund, meaning a higher proportion of retirees relative to active lives, the shorter its investment horizon, which directly lowers risk tolerance and shifts the allocation toward fixed income and away from riskier assets.
rationales.C: The effect runs in the positive direction. Youth extends liability duration and lengthens the horizon over which risk can be taken, so a young, largely active-lives plan has more rather than less capacity for risk. Lower tolerance belongs to the mature plan paying benefits to a large retiree population.

questions.stem: A defined benefit plan has a surplus of EUR 8 million on EUR 100 million of plan assets, liability duration of 20 years, a sponsor with low debt that remains profitable in a cyclical industry, and a workforce averaging age 39 with essentially no retirees. The plan's above-average risk tolerance is most likely attributable to:

options.B: its surplus, sponsor strength, and young workforce.
options.C: its sponsor's cyclical industry.

rationales.A: The plan is overfunded by EUR 8 million, a surplus equal to 8% of EUR 100 million in plan assets, so there is no deficit to close. The reasoning also reverses the direction of the relationship: poor funding status reduces risk tolerance rather than compelling risk taking, because a further investment loss would deepen the deficit and raise the contributions the sponsor must make.
rationales.B: Above-average risk tolerance here rests on several facts in combination: a small surplus of EUR 8 million, equal to 8% of EUR 100 million in plan assets, so the plan is overfunded; a strong sponsor balance sheet with low use of debt; a sponsor that is profitable despite operating in a cyclical industry; an average workforce age of 39, which is young; and an essentially active-lives plan with no retirees, consistent with the 20-year liability duration. The funding cushion absorbs losses, the low-debt and profitable sponsor has the capacity to contribute if needed, and the young active workforce gives a long horizon over which risk can be taken. Together these outweigh the one factor arguing the other way, the cyclicality of the sponsor's industry.
rationales.C: Cyclicality on its own argues for lower risk tolerance, not higher, because sponsor earnings weaken at the same time risky asset values fall, leaving the sponsor least able to contribute when the plan most needs it. The plan's above-average tolerance rests on the surplus, the low-debt balance sheet, the sponsor's profitability, and the young workforce, which together offset the cyclical industry rather than being caused by it.

questions.stem: If a defined benefit plan sponsor's revenues are highly cyclical, the plan's asset allocation most appropriately:

options.B: concentrates in the sponsor's industry.
options.C: avoids assets correlated with the sponsor's industry.

rationales.A: Correlated stress between sponsor and plan is precisely the risk to be managed, so sponsor cyclicality does bear on how plan assets are invested. A cyclical sponsor whose plan holds assets tied to the same cycle will face a demand for higher contributions in the same downturn that depresses its own revenues.
rationales.B: Concentration compounds the risk rather than exploiting the sponsor's expertise. A cyclical sponsor should avoid plan investments highly correlated with its core business, because a downturn would damage the sponsor's revenues and the plan's asset values at the same time, and funded status would deteriorate exactly when the sponsor can least afford to repair it.
rationales.C: If the plan sponsor's revenues are highly cyclical, it will not want plan funded status to deteriorate when the core business suffers from a cyclical downturn. In such cases the defined benefit plan's asset allocation would be modified to ensure adequate diversification, so as not to have significant exposure to assets highly correlated with the sponsor's core business or industry. In sum, it is desirable for plan assets to have low correlations with the sponsor's operating assets and high correlations with the plan's liabilities.

questions.stem: Longevity risk in a defined benefit pension plan is best described as:

options.A: a risk that participants outlive the plan's benefit assumptions.
options.B: a risk borne by insurers but not by pension plans.
options.C: a risk that no retirement system faces.

rationales.A: Longevity risk is the risk that an individual will live longer than expected and draw more in benefit payments than the amount determined in the calculation of plan liabilities. Retired workers therefore influence a plan's longevity risk directly. In private defined benefit pension plans the risk is pooled: if a participant dies earlier than expected, he or she leaves more assets in the pool, which can then cover additional payments for those who live longer than expected. This pooling does not, however, mitigate the effect of rising life expectancies across the participant population as a whole, which implies, all else equal, an increase in total defined benefit plan liabilities.
rationales.B: Defined benefit plans bear longevity risk directly. Retirees who live longer than assumed draw benefit payments beyond the amount provided for in the plan's liability calculation. Insurers that write annuities are exposed as well, but they are not the only bearers of the risk, and pooling within a plan does not remove it.
rationales.C: The risk is inherent in any promise of lifetime income, so it applies broadly: private defined benefit plans, state and social insurance retirement systems, and annuity providers all face it. Only a plan paying a fixed sum rather than a life-contingent benefit escapes it.

questions.stem: Poor defined benefit plan design most likely creates a risk of:

options.B: benefits too low to retain employees.
options.C: overly conservative contribution and return assumptions.

rationales.A: Poor plan design can create many risks for a private defined benefit plan sponsor. When setting out the formula for calculation of defined benefit payments, the sponsor must balance adequacy, meaning whether the benefit payment will be sufficient to meet income needs in retirement, against sustainability, meaning what contribution rate is sustainable and what investment return can realistically be achieved, within the context of its risk tolerance. There is a significant risk that a company will be overly optimistic in predicting its ability to make contributions to its pension plan decades into the future. The same optimism appears when pension design is used as an employee retention tool, or to address worker unrest by increasing future benefits instead of granting immediate pay raises, because the cost of the promise is deferred and understated at the moment it is made.
rationales.B: The design risk runs the other way. Sponsors are more likely to over-promise, using pension design as a retention tool and raising future benefits in place of current pay, than to set benefits so low that the plan fails to retain staff. Benefits that are too low are a failure on the adequacy side of the adequacy-sustainability trade-off; the risk the sponsor itself bears is the unsustainable promise.
rationales.C: The risk identified is over-optimism, not conservatism. Companies risk overestimating their ability to make contributions decades into the future, and overestimating the investment return that can realistically be achieved. Conservative contribution and return assumptions raise the measured cost of the plan today, but they cushion the sponsor later, so they act as a safeguard rather than as a design risk.

questions.stem: Detailed asset-liability management studies for defined benefit pension plans are most likely conducted:

options.B: daily.
options.C: every three to five years.

rationales.A: Many defined benefit pension plans do conduct these studies, on a cadence of every three to five years, using Monte Carlo simulation of thousands of scenarios for asset returns and for the factors driving liabilities. Liability values are not slow-moving either: the discount rate tracks market yields, so the funded ratio can shift materially between studies, which is part of why the study is repeated.
rationales.B: Daily monitoring of funded status and market risk is routine, but the full asset-liability management study is far less frequent. Simulating thousands of scenarios and then reworking contribution policy and the strategic asset allocation from the resulting distributions is a major exercise repeated every three to five years, not a daily revaluation cycle.
rationales.C: In setting overall investment strategy, many defined benefit pension plans engage in detailed asset-liability management studies every three to five years. These studies include Monte Carlo simulations of thousands of scenarios for asset returns and for the factors driving pension liabilities, importantly the discount rate, aimed at producing probability distributions for funded ratios and contribution rates at different horizons. Those distributions are useful for determining key metrics such as the expected funded ratio in 10 or 15 years, surplus volatility, surplus-at-risk, and the volatility of contribution rates.

drills.los_text: evaluate the investment policy statement of an institutional investor

questions.stem: A well-designed IPS most likely covers:

options.A: Mission, objectives, constraints, allocation policy, rebalancing, and reporting.
options.B: Portfolio construction mechanics alone.
options.C: The asset allocation policy alone.

rationales.A: The IPS is the governance charter for the whole investment program. Besides mission and investment objectives (that is, return requirement and risk tolerance), it should cover any constraints that affect the asset allocation, the asset allocation policy with ranges and asset class benchmarks, the rebalancing policy, guidelines affecting implementation of the asset allocation policy, and reporting requirements. It should be reviewed annually; revisions, however, should be infrequent, such as when material changes occur in investor circumstances and/or the market environment, as the IPS serves as the foundation for the investment program.
rationales.B: Security selection criteria and other portfolio construction mechanics sit below the IPS and are normally delegated to staff or external managers. The IPS itself is the comprehensive governance document: mission, return and risk objectives, constraints, allocation ranges with asset class benchmarks, rebalancing policy, implementation guidelines, and reporting. An IPS that specified construction detail alone would leave governance and objectives undocumented, which is precisely what the policy statement exists to prevent.
rationales.C: The asset allocation policy is one chapter of the IPS, not the whole of it. Mission, investment objectives in the form of a return requirement and a stated risk tolerance, constraints affecting the allocation, asset class benchmarks, rebalancing policy, implementation guidelines, and reporting requirements complete the document. The asset allocation policy and investment guidelines are typically placed in an appendix that can be modified more easily, but delegating them to an appendix is not the same as leaving mission, objectives, and rebalancing rules to separate operational documents.

questions.stem: IPS review and revision practices most likely are:

options.A: Reviewed every three to five years, with revisions made at each review.
options.B: Reviewed annually, with revisions reserved for material changes.
options.C: Reviewed quarterly, with revisions made at each review.

rationales.A: The review cycle is annual, not three to five years, and revisions are reserved for material changes in investor circumstances or in the market environment rather than made automatically at each review. A periodic asset-liability study may inform the asset allocation policy, but it does not set the cadence at which the policy statement is reviewed, and tying revision to the study would leave the document stale between studies.
rationales.B: The IPS should be reviewed annually; however, revisions should be infrequent, such as when material changes occur in investor circumstances and/or the market environment, as the IPS serves as the foundation for the investment program. The asset allocation policy and investment guidelines are typically included in an appendix that can be modified more easily, so routine implementation adjustments can be made without rewriting the policy statement itself.
rationales.C: Review is annual rather than quarterly, and revision should be infrequent. Revising the policy portfolio at every review would let short-term market movements drive the document that is meant to be the stable foundation of the investment program. Market movement is absorbed by the allocation ranges and by the rebalancing policy, and by the appendix holding allocation and guideline detail, not by rewriting the objectives each quarter.

questions.stem: A corporate defined benefit pension plan IPS most likely states its investment objective as seeking to:

options.B: Maximize long-term return subject to a low likelihood of missing a target funding level.
options.C: Minimize plan costs, whatever the return outcome.

rationales.A: Maximization is conditioned, not unqualified. The trustee wishes to ensure the plan can meet its obligations to the beneficiaries while recognizing the cost implications to the company of pursuing excessively conservative investment strategies, so the objective is to maximize the long-term return on investments subject to, in the trustee's opinion, an acceptably low likelihood of failing to achieve an ongoing 105% funding level. Strip the funding condition and the objective would license risk the plan cannot carry.
rationales.B: The objective is defined as wishing to maximize the long-term return on investments subject to, in the trustee's opinion, an acceptably low likelihood of failing to achieve an ongoing 105% funding level. That phrasing balances a sustainable long-term return against funded-ratio risk: return is pursued only within a tolerance expressed as the probability of falling short of the target funded ratio, which keeps the plan able to meet its obligations to beneficiaries while avoiding the cost to the sponsor of an excessively conservative strategy.
rationales.C: Cost minimization alone is not the objective. The trustee explicitly recognizes the cost implications to the company of pursuing excessively conservative strategies, but the objective itself is a maximized long-term return subject to an acceptably low likelihood of failing to achieve an ongoing 105% funding level. Minimizing cost regardless of return outcomes would push the plan toward the conservative stance the trustee is trying to avoid, and toward underfunding.

questions.stem: For a defined contribution plan participant who selects the growth option, the IPS investment objective is most likely to:

options.A: Outperform a composite benchmark by 1% annually while avoiding negative annual returns.
options.B: Outperform inflation by 4% over seven-year periods, accepting 4–6 negative years in 20.
options.C: Outperform inflation by 2% over three-year periods, accepting 1–2 negative years in 20.

rationales.A: A participant selecting the growth option indicates a higher risk tolerance over a longer investment time horizon, so the objective is framed relative to inflation over a long measurement period and states the risk being accepted rather than promising its absence. The objective is to build an investment portfolio to outperform inflation + 4% per annum over 7-year periods while accepting a high level of risk that is expected to generate 4–6 negative annual returns over any 20-year period. A 12-month relative-return target paired with a promise of no negative years describes neither the horizon nor the risk of a growth option, and no equity-dominated portfolio can honor the loss-avoidance pledge.
rationales.B: A participant selecting the growth option indicates a higher risk tolerance over a longer investment time horizon. The investment objective for the growth option is to build an investment portfolio to outperform inflation + 4% per annum over 7-year periods while accepting a high level of risk that is expected to generate 4–6 negative annual returns over any 20-year period. The statement captures all three elements a participant needs: the return target in real terms, the horizon over which it is to be judged, and transparency about the frequency of losing years that the target implies.
rationales.C: These are defensive-option parameters. The growth option targets inflation + 4% per annum, measured over 7-year periods, and accepts a high level of risk expected to generate 4–6 negative annual returns over any 20-year period. A real target of 2% over 3-year periods with only 1–2 negative years in 20 states a lower return objective, a shorter horizon, and a lower risk tolerance than the participant choosing growth has expressed.

questions.stem: A university endowment's IPS spending policy is most likely:
