options.A: A smoothed blend of prior-year spending and a long-term rate applied to average market values.
options.B: A fixed percentage of current market value each year.
options.C: No formal rule, with distributions left to the annual budget.

rationales.A: Under the policy, spending for a given year equals 80% of spending in the previous year, adjusted for inflation (CPI within a range of 0% and 6%), plus 20% of the long-term spending rate of 5.0% applied to the 12-quarter rolling average of market values. The hybrid rule has two implications. First, by incorporating the previous year's spending it eliminates large fluctuations and so enables the university to plan for operating budget needs. Second, by adjusting spending toward the long-term rate of 5.0%, it ensures spending levels remain sensitive to fluctuating market value levels, thereby providing stability in long-term purchasing power.
rationales.B: A flat percentage of current assets is not what the rule does. It blends 80% of the prior year's spending, adjusted for inflation with CPI bounded between 0% and 6%, with 20% of the 5.0% long-term spending rate applied to a 12-quarter rolling average of market values. Both devices exist to smooth: the prior-year term dampens year-to-year swings in the operating budget, and the 12-quarter average dampens the market value input itself. Applying 5% to the current market value every year would pass market volatility straight through to the budget.
rationales.C: A well-defined hybrid policy is specified, not left to annual discretion. Spending equals 80% of the previous year's spending, inflation-adjusted with CPI bounded at 0% and 6%, plus 20% of the 5.0% long-term spending rate applied to the 12-quarter rolling average of market values. A written rule is what lets the university plan its operating budget and preserves long-term purchasing power; ad hoc annual distributions would do neither.

questions.stem: An endowment IPS built on equity dominance and a preference for illiquid private investments most likely sets its fixed income and cash allocation range at:

rationales.A: Fixed income and cash is 5%–15%, benchmarked to the Citigroup US Treasury Index. A 30%–50% fixed income range is inconsistent with an equity-dominant, alternatives-heavy policy portfolio: global equity 20%–40%, private equity and venture capital 15%–25%, private real estate 5%–15%, real assets 5%–15%, and absolute return strategies 15%–25% already claim the bulk of the portfolio, and a bond sleeve of a third to a half could not coexist with them.
rationales.B: The policy ranges are global equity 20%–40% (MSCI World Index); private equity and venture capital 15%–25% (Cambridge Associates LLC US Private Equity Index); private real estate 5%–15% (NCREIF Property Index); real assets 5%–15% (annualized CPI-U + 5%); absolute return strategies 15%–25% (HFRI Fund of Funds Index); and fixed income and cash 5%–15% (Citigroup US Treasury Index). The long-term custom benchmark weights are 30% MSCI World, 20% Cambridge Associates, 10% NCREIF, 10% CPI-U + 5%, 20% HFRI, and 10% Citigroup Treasury. A small fixed income and cash sleeve follows directly from the stated principles: equities are expected to be the highest-performing asset class over the long term and will dominate, and private illiquid investments are expected to outperform more-liquid public investments.
rationales.C: Fixed income and cash is only 5%–15%, not a quarter to a third of the portfolio. The rest of the allocation confirms the shape: the equity range is 20%–40% benchmarked to the global MSCI World Index rather than 40%–60% against the S&P 500, private equity and venture capital is 15%–25%, private real estate and real assets are 5%–15% each, and absolute return strategies are 15%–25%. An endowment that expects equities and illiquid private assets to drive long-term return does not park 25%–35% in Treasuries.

questions.stem: The core investment principles stated in an endowment's IPS most likely are:

options.A: Equity dominance, illiquid assets, home-market orientation, and concentration.
options.B: Equity dominance, illiquid assets, global orientation, and diversification.
options.C: Equity dominance, liquidity preference, global orientation, and diversification.

rationales.A: The third and fourth principles are the opposite of a home-market tilt and concentration. The endowment will consider the broadest possible set of investment opportunities in its search for attractive risk/return profiles, which is a global orientation. And thoughtful diversification within and between asset classes by region, sector, and economic source of return can lower volatility and raise compound returns over the long term, which is why diversification, not concentration, is the stated principle.
rationales.B: The four principles are equity dominance, equities being expected to be the highest-performing asset class over the long term and thus dominating the portfolio; illiquid assets, since private illiquid investments are in general expected to outperform more-liquid public investments by exploiting market inefficiencies; global orientation, the endowment considering the broadest possible set of investment opportunities in its search for attractive risk/return profiles; and diversification, thoughtful diversification within and between asset classes by region, sector, and economic source of return being able to lower volatility and raise compound returns over the long term.
rationales.C: The second principle is the reverse of a liquidity preference. Private illiquid investments are expected to outperform more-liquid public investments by exploiting market inefficiencies, which is why the endowment accepts illiquidity rather than paying for liquidity it does not need. An endowment with a perpetual horizon and a smoothed spending rule is one of the few investors able to harvest that premium, so a stated preference for liquidity would forfeit return the portfolio is built to earn.

questions.stem: Reporting required by an institutional investor's IPS is most likely:

options.B: Quarterly and trailing-period performance attribution, asset allocation, and market value.
options.C: A single annual statement.

rationales.A: Reporting is a standard component of the IPS. The investment team, with the oversight of management, must provide adequate reporting to the board of trustees, the investment committee, and other stakeholders; a policy statement that imposed no reporting obligation would leave those bodies unable to carry out the oversight the governance structure assigns them.
rationales.B: The reporting structure should include performance measurement and attribution for the quarter and trailing periods for the portfolio, both in absolute terms and relative to the established benchmarks; the asset allocation of the total portfolio; and the market value of the total portfolio. These are provided to the board of trustees, the investment committee, and other stakeholders, and together they let the oversight bodies see what was earned, how it compared with the policy benchmarks, where the assets now sit against the policy ranges, and the size of the portfolio.
rationales.C: The cadence is quarterly and trailing-period, not a single annual statement, and the content is performance measurement and attribution in both absolute and benchmark-relative terms, plus the asset allocation and market value of the total portfolio. Reporting once a year would not let the board of trustees or the investment committee act on drift from the policy ranges or on manager underperformance while either still mattered.

drills.los_text: evaluate the investment portfolio of a private DB plan, sovereign wealth fund, university endowment, and private foundation

questions.stem: For a DB pension plan, the primary investment objective most likely is:

options.A: To pursue no explicit return target.
options.B: To minimize risk regardless of funding requirements.
options.C: To earn a long-term nominal return sufficient to meet contractual liabilities.

rationales.A: A long-term target return, usually defined in nominal terms, anchors the objective. It is set over a specified investment horizon of 3–5 years or even as long as 10 or 25 years, with an appropriate level of risk that allows the plan to meet its contractual liabilities. Without a target return there is nothing against which to judge the risk taken or the contributions required.
rationales.B: Risk minimization on its own cannot meet the liabilities. The primary objective is a long-term target return, usually nominal, over a specified investment horizon of 3–5 years or even as long as 10 or 25 years, carried at an appropriate level of risk that allows the plan to meet its contractual liabilities. Funding requirements are the constraint that fixes how much risk is appropriate, so an objective that ignores them inverts the problem: a minimum-risk portfolio would raise the present value of expected cash contributions, which the secondary objective seeks to minimize.
rationales.C: The primary objective for a defined benefit pension plan is to achieve a long-term target return, usually defined in nominal terms, over a specified investment horizon of 3–5 years or even as long as 10 or 25 years, with an appropriate level of risk that allows the plan to meet its contractual liabilities. The secondary objective could be to minimize the present value of expected cash contributions.

questions.stem: Across major national pension markets, asset allocations most likely show:

options.A: Japan leading the move into alternative assets.
options.B: Japan and the Netherlands holding the largest defined contribution and equity shares.
options.C: Australia and the United States holding the largest defined contribution and equity shares.

rationales.A: Japan has been the slowest of these countries to increase allocations to alternatives. The transition is underway — the country's largest plan, the Government Pension Investment Fund, is reducing its allocation to domestic bonds in favor of alternatives — but it began from a bond-heavy allocation and from behind, not in front.
rationales.B: Australia and the United States, not Japan and the Netherlands, have the largest proportions of defined contribution pension assets and the largest allocations to equities. Japanese allocations remain bond-heavy, and Japan has been the slowest of these countries to increase allocations to alternatives, although its largest plan is now shifting out of domestic bonds. The Netherlands does sit among the countries with the highest proportion of its equity allocation invested domestically, but a home bias in equities is a different matter from the size of the equity or the defined contribution share.
rationales.C: Average asset allocations differ very widely by country. Australia and the United States have the largest proportions of defined contribution pension assets and also the largest allocations to equities. The United States, Australia, and the Netherlands have the highest proportions of their equity allocations invested in their local markets; given the size of the domestic equity markets in Australia and the Netherlands, that implies significant home bias. Japan, by contrast, has been the slowest of these countries to increase allocations to alternatives, though the transition is underway as the Government Pension Investment Fund reduces its allocation to domestic bonds in favor of alternatives.

questions.stem: US corporate defined benefit pension plans increased their fixed-income allocations over the past decade most likely to:

options.B: Reduce funded ratio volatility.
options.C: Capture high expected fixed-income returns.

rationales.A: No regulatory mandate drove the shift. The reallocation was a liability-driven investing choice: corporate plans accepted low expected returns in exchange for assets whose value moves with the present value of the pension liability, which is what dampens funded ratio volatility.
rationales.B: Over the past decade US corporate pension plans increased their allocations to fixed income despite low expected returns, driven by the desire to reduce their funded ratio volatility. Lengthening and matching the fixed-income portfolio to the liability under a liability-driven approach makes the surplus or deficit far less sensitive to interest rate moves, because the assets and the discounted liability then reprice together. Contrast US public pension plans, which reduced their fixed-income allocations overall while shifting within fixed income toward high yield, riskier bonds. That repositioning is driven by the large gap that has opened between their expected rate of return and the yield available on long-term government securities.
rationales.C: Expected returns on fixed income were low over this period, not high, and that was precisely the cost corporate plans chose to accept in order to control funded ratio volatility. It was the public plans facing a gap between their assumed rate of return and long-term government yields that moved the other way, into high yield bonds, in search of return.

questions.stem: The shift from equities to alternatives in pension portfolios is most likely motivated by:

options.A: Fees below those of passive index funds.
options.B: Equity-like long-run returns with low drawdowns.
options.C: Better daily liquidity than public equities.

rationales.A: Alternatives carry high fees. Management fees plus performance fees on private equity, private debt, real estate and hedge funds run well above those of passive index funds, so cost savings cannot be the motive. The motivation is the perceived return and diversification profile: equity-like returns over the long run with relatively low drawdowns and low or negative correlations with traditional investments.
rationales.B: The alternatives category covers private equity and debt markets, real estate, hedge funds and real assets. As a group these assets tend to have low, or negative, correlations with traditional investments as well as lower drawdowns. For hedge funds that may be explained by the lower volatility of these strategies versus equity markets. Private asset classes have historically also exhibited lower drawdowns than equities, which may be partially explained by a lack of fully marking-to-market, because market transactions are limited, and by appraisal-based valuations that lag changes in market pricing. Overall, the perception of institutional investors is that alternatives can produce equity-like returns over the long run with relatively low drawdowns, and that perception has been the motivation for the shift from equities to alternatives over the past decade and a half.
rationales.C: Private market investments are notably illiquid rather than liquid. Private equity, real estate and hedge fund positions transact infrequently and come with lock-ups, gates and multi-year capital commitments, so daily liquidity is worse than that of public equities. Illiquidity is a cost the allocation accepts in exchange for an expected premium, not the reason for making it.

questions.stem: Over the period from 2005 to 2017, the asset allocation of US university endowments larger than US$1 billion most likely:

options.B: Increased its allocation to alternatives.
options.C: Left its allocation to alternatives unchanged.

rationales.A: The move ran in the opposite direction. Average allocations to alternatives at endowments of more than US$1 billion rose from 39% at the end of June 2005 to 60% at the end of June 2017; the sleeves that were cut were public equities and fixed income, not alternatives.
rationales.B: Average asset allocations at US university endowments of more than US$1 billion in size show that over this period the largest endowments significantly increased their allocation to alternatives, from 39% at the end of June 2005 to 60% at the end of June 2017. That increase came at the expense of the two traditional sleeves: public equities were reduced from 45% to 30% and fixed income from 14% to 11%. This is the endowment model in practice, with a long horizon, no near-term liability matching requirement, and a willingness to accept illiquidity in return for an expected premium and access to top-quartile private managers.
rationales.C: The shift was substantial rather than static: a 21 percentage point increase in alternatives, from 39% to 60%, funded by cutting public equities from 45% to 30% and fixed income from 14% to 11%.

questions.stem: Over the 10 years ending June 2020, annual returns on US endowments of more than US$1 billion, relative to returns on endowments of less than US$500 million, were most likely:

options.B: Lower.
options.C: The same.

rationales.A: Larger endowments have generally been able to generate higher returns over this period. Endowments of more than US$1 billion have generated anywhere between 50 bps and 60 bps higher returns annually than the smaller endowments holding less than US$500 million. A gap of that size compounds into a significant difference over a 10-year period, and those higher returns have allowed the larger endowments to pay out a larger part of their assets to support their universities. The usual explanations are advantages of scale: an internal investment staff, access to capacity-constrained private managers, and the balance sheet strength to fund long lock-ups.
rationales.B: The direction is reversed. The larger endowments outperformed the smaller ones by roughly 50 bps to 60 bps a year over the decade rather than lagging them.
rationales.C: The differential was real rather than zero. It ran at about 50 bps to 60 bps a year in favour of endowments of more than US$1 billion, which compounds to a significant gap over a 10-year period.

questions.stem: The liquidity risk that the endowment model exposed during the 2007-2009 global financial crisis is best described as:

options.A: Excess liquidity that could not be deployed.
options.B: A shortfall that forced sales and borrowing.
options.C: No material liquidity strain.

rationales.A: The crisis produced the opposite problem, a liquidity shortfall. Endowments weighted toward alternatives met capital calls from private funds, collapsing distributions and spending commitments to their universities all at once, while the liquid part of the portfolio had fallen in value. Several were pushed into secondary sales of private fund interests at marked-down prices and into emergency borrowing; none were constrained by surplus cash.
rationales.B: Most large endowments follow the endowment investment model and rely heavily on alternative investments to achieve their long-term investment objectives, and that approach is not without risks. During the global financial crisis several large endowments faced significant liquidity challenges and were forced to do one or more of three things: sell portions of their private investment portfolios in the secondary markets, reduce payouts to their universities, or issue bonds to bridge their liquidity needs. The rapid post-crisis recovery arguably bailed out many endowments, but had the crisis lasted longer the pain would have been substantially worse. David Swensen, the longtime CIO of the Yale endowment, and his colleagues have regularly warned against a blanket application of the endowment model for this reason.
rationales.C: Liquidity stress was severe rather than absent. Unfunded capital commitments kept coming due as distributions dried up, and marked-down liquid assets had to be sold, which is why some endowments resorted to secondary market sales of private holdings, reduced payouts or bond issuance.

questions.stem: The investment strategy of a sovereign wealth development fund is most likely to:

options.A: Invest exclusively outside the domestic economy.
options.B: Operate without a development mandate.
options.C: Support national economic development.

rationales.A: A development fund's focus is domestic. It invests in essential infrastructure, innovation or key industries at home in order to raise the country's economic growth or diversify its economy, and its implicit target is stated in terms of real domestic GDP growth and productivity. A portfolio invested only abroad would defeat that mandate.
rationales.B: A development mandate is the defining feature of this fund type, so an absence of one describes no development fund at all. Stabilization, savings, reserve and pension reserve funds are the sovereign wealth fund categories defined by other objectives; the development fund is the one whose objective is the domestic economy.
rationales.C: Development funds are established to support a nation's economic development through investing in essential infrastructure and innovation, or by supporting key industries. Their liabilities are not clearly defined and are typically uncertain, but their overall objective is to raise a country's economic growth or to diversify the economy. As such, these funds have an implicit real return target: to increase real domestic GDP growth and productivity. Some initiatives, such as infrastructure or industrial development, may be ongoing and long-term, while others may have a fixed, medium-term horizon, such as a medical research fund. Mubadala Development Corp. of the UAE and the National Development Fund of Iran are examples.

questions.stem: A sovereign wealth savings fund is most likely characterized by:

options.B: A portfolio invested only in cash.
options.C: The absence of any return target.

rationales.A: Savings funds are typically established to transform proceeds from the sale of non-renewable natural resources into long-term wealth and a diversified portfolio of financial assets. The mission of a savings fund is wealth transfer to future generations after the sources of natural wealth have been depleted, so its liabilities are long-term. Some savings funds have a real return objective or an explicit spending policy, much like endowments. Because of their long horizons, savings funds invest in risky and illiquid assets, including equities and a wide range of alternative investments. They should, of course, avoid investing in assets highly correlated with the non-renewable resources from which the government is trying to diversify, since that correlation would reintroduce the exposure the fund exists to reduce.
rationales.B: An all-cash portfolio would be wrong for this mandate. The long horizon and the absence of near-term liabilities let savings funds hold risky and illiquid assets, including equities and a wide range of alternative investments, in pursuit of a real return objective; cash would not grow resource proceeds into intergenerational wealth.
rationales.C: Return targets are normally present. Some savings funds carry an explicit real return objective or a stated spending policy, in the manner of an endowment, because the purpose is to preserve and grow purchasing power for generations that will follow the depletion of the natural resource.

questions.stem: The strategic asset allocation of a sovereign wealth reserve fund most likely consists of:

options.B: Mainly equity and equity-equivalent investments.
options.C: No equity or equity-equivalent investments.

rationales.A: Holding only foreign exchange reserves describes the central bank's own reserve portfolio, not a reserve fund. A reserve fund exists precisely to earn a return above the yield on central bank reserves, which is why 50% to 70% of it sits in equity or equity-equivalent investments, with the remainder in liquid fixed income that can be sold if central bank reserves must be replenished.
rationales.B: Reserve funds typically hold 50% to 70% in equity or equity-equivalent investments to achieve their return targets. The remainder is likely to be invested in liquid fixed-income securities that could be readily sold should a dramatic change in the balance of trade require additional central bank reserves. Their horizons are long, but their liquidity needs sit above those of a savings fund and below those of a stabilization fund, which is why the fixed-income sleeve is kept liquid rather than illiquid. Examples of reserve funds include China Investment Corporation, Korea Investment Corporation, and GIC Private Limited of Singapore, formerly the Government of Singapore Investment Corporation.
rationales.C: Equity is the core of the allocation rather than absent from it. Reserve funds typically hold 50% to 70% in equity or equity-equivalent investments to reach their return targets, with liquid fixed income making up the balance.

questions.stem: The portfolios of budget stabilization funds most likely emphasize:

options.B: Cash and high-grade liquid fixed income.
options.C: Risk assets, with no cash holding.

rationales.A: The purpose of a stabilization fund, bridging government revenue shortfalls on short notice, rules out an equity-dominated portfolio. A negative commodity price shock would hit the budget and the equity portfolio at the same time, forcing sales into a drawdown exactly when the money is needed. The allocation is therefore conservative and liquid rather than growth-maximizing.
rationales.B: Stabilization funds must maintain a high level of liquidity and invest in assets that have a low risk of significant losses over short time periods. In the event of a negative commodity price shock, for example, the government might experience a significant budget deficit caused by lower commodity-based revenues; to stabilize the budget and meet spending needs, the stabilization fund's assets must be readily accessible. As a result, budget stabilization funds invest a significant portion of their portfolios in cash and high-grade, fixed-income instruments that are very liquid and carry little risk of significant drawdown. This also gives them the shortest effective investment horizon of the sovereign wealth fund types.
rationales.C: Cash and high-grade liquid fixed income dominate precisely because a drawdown must be avoidable at need. A fund holding no cash would have to sell impaired risk assets to fund a budget deficit, which is the outcome the fund exists to prevent.

questions.stem: The asset allocation of a pension reserve fund most likely:

options.B: Holds significant equities during accumulation.
options.C: Holds one allocation across both phases.

rationales.A: Pension reserve funds have long horizons before withdrawals begin, so a permanently short-term portfolio would sacrifice the growth needed to meet future pension and health care liabilities. The allocation is phase-dependent: equities and relatively illiquid investments while assets accumulate, then liquid high-quality fixed income once decumulation starts.
rationales.B: Pension reserve funds need to meet future pension or health care liabilities when they come due, and depending on when significant fund withdrawals are expected, liquidity needs change over time. During the accumulation phase, reserve funds can hold a significant part of their portfolios in equities and relatively illiquid investments, because no near-term outflows compete with them. Once the decumulation phase begins, the asset allocation will gradually shift toward more liquid, high-quality, fixed-income investments. The Future Fund of Australia illustrates the growth orientation of the accumulation phase: its investment mandate is to achieve an average annual return of at least the Consumer Price Index plus 4% to 5% per year over the long term, with acceptable risk.
rationales.C: A single static allocation would ignore the change in liquidity needs over the fund's life. The portfolio holds equities and relatively illiquid assets while contributions accumulate, then transitions gradually toward liquid, high-quality fixed income as withdrawals begin.

questions.stem: Compared with university endowments, US private grant-making foundations are most likely characterized by:

options.A: no material differences in investment management.
options.B: a similar investment philosophy but lower liquidity needs.
options.C: a similar investment philosophy but higher liquidity needs.

rationales.A: The investment philosophies are indeed similar, but the two institution types are not managed identically. US private grant-making foundations are legally required to pay out 5% of assets, measured on a trailing 12-month basis, plus investment expenses; university endowments have no such legal mandate and operate under more-flexible spending rules. That difference in liabilities feeds through to liquidity needs, which are higher for foundations. Foundations are also more likely to pursue mission-related or impact investing: the Ford Foundation allocated up to US$1.0 billion, more than 8% of assets, over 10 years to investments connected to its mission of addressing global inequality.
rationales.B: The direction is reversed. Foundations and endowments both typically have perpetual investment horizons and both invest to maintain purchasing power, but foundation payouts are not discretionary. In the United States, private grant-making foundations are legally required to pay out 5% of assets on a trailing 12-month basis plus investment expenses, while university endowments have more-flexible spending rules. The mandatory distribution means foundations generally carry higher, not lower, liquidity needs, and it constrains how much illiquidity a foundation can hold relative to an otherwise comparable endowment.
rationales.C: In practice the investment philosophy of private foundations is typically similar to that of university endowments, despite important differences between them in terms of liabilities and liquidity needs. Both typically have perpetual investment horizons and both invest to maintain purchasing power. However, foundations generally have higher liquidity needs: in the United States, private grant-making foundations are legally required to pay out 5% of assets, on a trailing 12-month basis, plus investment expenses, whereas university endowments have more-flexible spending rules. Foundations may also pursue mission-related or impact investing alongside the return objective, as when the Ford Foundation allocated up to US$1.0 billion, more than 8% of assets, over 10 years to investments related to its mission of addressing global inequality.

questions.stem: Relative to the boards of university endowments, the boards of private foundations are most likely:

options.A: more likely to include investment professionals.
options.B: equally likely to include investment professionals.
options.C: less likely to include investment professionals.

rationales.A: Reversed. University endowments typically have alumni sitting on their boards, people with a special relationship to the university who may also bring significant financial market skills, for example in private equity or hedge funds. Board members for foundations, by contrast, are typically individuals involved with grant making and not necessarily investment professionals, so investment expertise is generally thinner on a foundation board, not deeper.
rationales.B: The two board profiles are distinct rather than interchangeable. Endowment boards draw on alumni who combine a special relationship to the institution with potentially significant financial market skills, while foundation boards are typically populated by individuals involved with grant making. The skill-set gap is the point of the comparison, and it matters because it affects the quality of board oversight, how much decision making is delegated to investment staff, and ultimately the quality of investment decisions.
rationales.C: The boards of foundations tend to differ from the boards of endowments in skill set. University endowments typically have alumni sitting on their boards, people with a special relationship to the university and who may have significant financial market skills, for example in private equity or hedge funds. Board members for foundations, however, are typically individuals involved with grant making and not necessarily investment professionals. This difference in skill sets may affect the quality of board oversight, the level of delegation of decision making to investment staff, and the quality of investment decisions.

drills.los_text: describe considerations affecting the balance sheet management of banks and insurers

questions.stem: The largest component of the assets of large international banks is most likely:

options.B: debt securities.
options.C: equity securities.

rationales.A: The largest component of bank assets is loans, typically comprising up to 50% or more of the assets of the large, international banks that dominate the sector. The next largest component is debt securities, typically accounting for 25% or more of total assets. The largest remaining portion consists of currency, deposits with central banks such as the Bank of Japan or the Bank of England, receivables, and bullion. The loan book is therefore the primary driver of a bank's credit exposure, and the securities portfolio is managed around it.
rationales.B: The ordering is reversed. Loans are the largest component, typically up to 50% or more of assets for the large international banks that dominate the sector, and debt securities are the next largest at typically 25% or more of total assets. Debt securities are substantial, but they sit second, not first, and the roughly 50%/25% split runs the other way from what this option states.
rationales.C: Equity holdings are a minor component of a bank balance sheet, not its largest. After loans, typically up to 50% or more of assets, and debt securities, typically 25% or more, the remainder consists mainly of currency, deposits with central banks, receivables, and bullion. Trading and investment operations do not dominate the asset mix of the large international banks that dominate the sector.

questions.stem: The largest component of a bank's liabilities is most likely:

options.B: wholesale funding.
options.C: shareholder equity.

rationales.A: Banks' liabilities are comprised of deposits and also include short-term funding, such as commercial paper, as well as longer-term debt. Deposits are the largest component, usually more than half of total liabilities. They fall into two groups: time or term deposits, interest-bearing accounts with a specified maturity date, a category that includes savings accounts and certificates of deposit; and demand deposits, which can be drawn upon regularly and without notice through checking accounts and online or ATM-accessible savings. Beyond deposits, banks access wholesale funding such as Federal Funds, public funds, and other government-supported short-term vehicles. Other liabilities comprise long-term debt at 10%-15% of the total balance sheet and items such as trading and securities payables and repurchase finance payables, on the order of 10%-20% of balance sheet liabilities.
rationales.B: Wholesale funding is real but secondary. Deposits are the largest component of bank liabilities, usually more than half of the total, and wholesale sources such as Federal Funds, public funds, and other government-supported short-term vehicles supplement them rather than replace them. A bank funded entirely in wholesale and interbank markets would also be running exactly the funding profile that post-crisis liquidity rules were written to discourage.
rationales.C: Equity is a thin slice of a bank's balance sheet, and deposit-taking is the core of the business rather than something prohibited. Time deposits, including savings accounts and certificates of deposit, and demand deposits together usually fund more than half of total liabilities, with long-term debt adding 10%-15% and trading, securities and repurchase finance payables another 10%-20%. Post-crisis capital rules raised required capital ratios; they did not convert bank funding into equity or bar banks from accepting deposits.

questions.stem: A bank's tactical investment horizon is most likely:

options.B: undefined.
options.C: shorter than that of other financial institutions.

rationales.A: The two horizons diverge sharply. The tactical investment horizon for a bank's investment portfolio is directly impacted by the nature and maturities of its asset base and liability structure, which are short. The strategic horizon, by contrast, is perpetuity because of the bank's corporate structure, making it as long as or longer than that of many defined benefit plans, endowments, foundations, and sovereign wealth funds. A perpetual strategic horizon sitting on top of a short tactical horizon is the defining tension in bank portfolio management.
rationales.B: The tactical horizon exists and is the operative constraint. It is set directly by the nature and maturities of the bank's asset base and liability structure, and the instruments held in a bank portfolio tend to have far shorter maturities than those held by other financial institutions. What is long is the strategic horizon, which is perpetuity given the corporate structure.
rationales.C: The tactical investment horizon for a bank's investment portfolio is directly impacted by the nature and maturities of its asset base and liability structure. Although commercial banks, as corporations, have a perpetual time horizon, possibly longer than that of other institutions, the instruments held in a bank portfolio tend to have far shorter maturities than those held by other financial institutions. The strategic horizon is perpetuity because of the corporate structure, which makes it as long as, or longer than, many defined benefit plans, endowments, foundations, and sovereign wealth funds; the tactical horizon is where the short maturities bind.

questions.stem: Since the global financial crisis, regulation of bank liquidity has most likely:

options.B: loosened the liquidity requirements already in place.
options.C: tightened requirements through mandated liquidity coverage ratios.

rationales.A: Mandated liquidity coverage ratios and net stable funding ratios are precisely the new requirements introduced after the crisis. Liquidity coverage ratios require that highly liquid assets constitute more than 100% of highly probable near-term expected cash outflows, and net stable funding ratios set minimum requirements for stable funding sources, including capital, long-term debt, and non-volatile deposits, relative to assets.
rationales.B: Requirements tightened rather than loosened. Prior to 2007-2009, deficiencies in deposit funding were made up with wholesale funding and banks used their portfolios as a source of return, investing in lower-quality, less liquid securities. Post-crisis, bank portfolios are increasingly comprised of higher-quality, more liquid securities, driven by increased regulatory scrutiny on a global basis. Liquidity coverage ratios now demand highly liquid assets above 100% of highly probable near-term expected cash outflows, which is a binding constraint on portfolio composition, not an encouragement to lend more freely.
rationales.C: Bank liquidity needs have evolved since the global financial crisis of 2007-2009. Before that period, deficiencies in liquidity from deposits were made up with wholesale funding, and banks used their portfolios as a source of return, so they were invested in lower-quality, less liquid securities. In the post-crisis environment, bank portfolios are increasingly comprised of higher-quality, more liquid securities. This trend toward more conservative management has largely been driven by increased regulatory scrutiny on a global basis, most noticeably through the introduction of mandated liquidity coverage ratios and net stable funding ratios. Liquidity coverage ratios require that highly liquid assets constitute more than 100% of highly probable near-term expected cash outflows; net stable funding ratios set minimum requirements for stable funding sources relative to assets, with such stable sources including capital, long-term debt, and non-volatile deposits.

questions.stem: In 2021, a consortium of 26 global financial institutions provided Anheuser-Busch InBev with a USD 10.1 billion, five-year facility addressing brewery water efficiency, recycled PET content, RE100 renewable electricity, and greenhouse gas reduction. The financing is most likely a:

options.B: green bond with ring-fenced use of proceeds.
options.C: credit-rating-linked revolving credit facility.

rationales.A: During the first quarter of 2021, ING together with Santander coordinated one of the largest sustainability-linked revolving credit facilities ever issued. Anheuser-Busch InBev, a multinational drinks and brewing company, was provided a USD 10.1 billion revolving credit facility with a five-year term by a consortium of 26 leading global financial institutions. The pricing mechanism incentivizes the company to address four key performance areas aligned with its sustainability goals: further improving water efficiency at its breweries globally; increasing recycled content in PET primary packaging; sourcing purchased electricity from renewable sources as outlined in the RE100 commitment; and reducing greenhouse gas emissions as part of its science-based Climate Action Goal. The sustainability linkage runs through the cost of the loan, so performance against the key performance indicators feeds directly into the spread paid.
rationales.B: This was a sustainability-linked facility, not a use-of-proceeds instrument. A green bond restricts contractually how the money raised may be spent, project by project; a sustainability-linked loan leaves the borrower free to use the funds for general corporate purposes and instead varies the pricing with measured performance against agreed key performance indicators. Here the borrower's spread moves with water efficiency at the breweries, recycled PET content, RE100 renewable electricity sourcing, and greenhouse gas reduction under the Climate Action Goal, and the instrument was a revolving credit facility arranged by a bank consortium rather than a bond sold to investors.
rationales.C: The pricing mechanism is tied to sustainability performance, not to the borrower's credit rating. The facility rewards or penalizes Anheuser-Busch InBev on four key performance areas: brewery water efficiency, recycled content in PET primary packaging, renewable electricity sourcing under the RE100 commitment, and greenhouse gas reduction under the science-based Climate Action Goal. A rating-based ratchet, common in conventional loan documentation, would make the spread a function of agency action rather than of the borrower's own measured environmental outcomes, which is the whole point of the sustainability-linked structure.

questions.stem: The bearer of investment risk on an insurance product is most likely:

options.A: the company, for every product type.
options.B: the policyholder, for every product type.
options.C: the company for fixed products and the policyholder for variable products.

rationales.A: Variable products shift the investment risk to the policyholder. Variable life insurance and variable annuities are written in a separate account, where the policyholder takes the investment outcome; only whole life, term life, universal life, and fixed annuities leave the risk with the company in its general account. The bearer therefore varies by product rather than resting with the insurer in all cases.
rationales.B: For whole life, term life, universal life insurance, and fixed annuities, the company bears the investment risk and the assets sit in the general account. The policyholder bears it only for variable life insurance and variable annuities, which are written in a separate account. Because the bearer differs across the product shelf, no single party can be said to bear the risk on every product.
rationales.C: The main investment risk bearer differs by product. Whole life, term life, universal life insurance, and fixed annuities put the investment risk on the company, and the supporting assets are held in the general account, where the insurer has guaranteed a benefit or a crediting rate and must fund it regardless of market outcomes. Variable life insurance and variable annuities put the investment risk on the policyholder, and those assets are held in a separate account, segregated from the general account, with the policyholder taking the gains and losses of the chosen sub-accounts. The account structure follows from who bears the investment risk, which is why general account portfolios are managed against guaranteed liabilities while separate account portfolios are managed to the policyholder's own mandate.

questions.stem: The stakeholders of an insurance company most likely include:

options.B: shareholders only.
options.C: internal parties only.

rationales.A: The stakeholders of insurers include external parties such as shareholders, derivatives counterparties, policyholders, creditors, regulators, and rating agencies, as well as internal parties such as employees, management, and boards of directors. The insurance industry is tightly regulated in most countries, usually by state or national authorities. The rating agencies, including A.M. Best, Standard & Poor's, Moody's, and Fitch, are stakeholders in the management of insurance investment portfolios because they monitor the financial stability of insurance companies and provide credit ratings and data on the industry to the investment community globally. Each of these parties constrains portfolio choices in a different way, which is why an insurer's investment policy has to answer to more than one audience at once.
rationales.B: The stakeholder set is much broader than the shareholder register. Alongside shareholders sit derivatives counterparties, policyholders, creditors, regulators, and rating agencies on the external side, and employees, management, and boards of directors internally. Policyholders have a direct claim on the insurer's ability to pay, regulators set the capital and reserving rules the portfolio is managed against, and the rating agencies publish the credit ratings that determine the insurer's own cost of funding, so none of them can be treated as outside the stakeholder set.
rationales.C: Insurers face extensive external oversight. Policyholders, creditors, derivatives counterparties, shareholders, regulators, and rating agencies are all external stakeholders, and the industry is tightly regulated in most countries, usually by state or national authorities. The rating agencies, including A.M. Best, Standard & Poor's, Moody's, and Fitch, monitor the financial stability of insurance companies and publish ratings and industry data to the global investment community, which makes their views a live constraint on how the investment portfolio is run.

questions.stem: In modeling the natural hazard risk of its real estate portfolio, an insurer's three risk components are most likely:

options.A: hazard, exposure, and correlation with the equity portfolio.
options.B: hazard, exposure, and vulnerability.
options.C: hazard, premium adequacy, and reinsurance capacity.

rationales.A: The third component is vulnerability, not correlation with financial portfolios. Vulnerability is defined by destruction rates, as a function of the hazard and the exposure, and it is what turns a given storm or flood striking a given building into an expected loss figure. Correlation with the equity portfolio matters for total enterprise risk, but it is not one of the three components of a natural hazard model.
rationales.B: Models that assess the risk of natural hazards consider three components: the hazard, as defined by its severity and frequency; the exposure, as characterized by the building's physical properties; and the vulnerability, as defined by destruction rates, a function of the hazard and the exposure. AXA, a French multinational insurer, reported that as of the end of 2020 the annual average losses for its real estate portfolio were estimated at EUR 4.3 million from floods and EUR 6.2 million from windstorms. Risk evaluation of this kind naturally evolves to consider potential financial impacts under various published climate scenarios, such as the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change's Representative Concentration Pathways 2.6 and 8.5.
rationales.C: Premium adequacy and reinsurance capacity are underwriting and capital management concerns on the liability side of the insurer, not components of a physical hazard model. The model's three components are the hazard, defined by severity and frequency; the exposure, characterized by the building's physical properties; and the vulnerability, defined by destruction rates as a function of the hazard and the exposure. Those three combine into an annual average loss estimate for the property portfolio, which can then be run through climate scenarios such as Representative Concentration Pathways 2.6 and 8.5.
